Not long ago, remembering a friend's telephone number was an ordinary task; today many people cannot recall even their own. Psychologists call the habit of handing information to external devices cognitive offloading, and it is hardly new. Scribes kept ledgers, navigators relied on charts, and merchants trusted their account books rather than their memories. What has changed is the scale and speed of the outsourcing. In an influential series of experiments published in 2011, Betsy Sparrow and her colleagues found that participants who believed a piece of trivia would be saved on a computer were less likely to remember the fact itself, though they were often able to recall the folder in which it had been stored. ____, the mind appeared to treat the computer as an external hard drive, retaining the path to the information rather than the information itself.
Whether this habit is cause for alarm remains contested. Critics warn that a memory accustomed to delegation may grow lazy, leaving people less able to connect ideas they never genuinely absorbed. Defenders counter that the practice frees scarce mental resources for reasoning and creativity, much as a calculator spares us tedious arithmetic. The more sensible conclusion may be that delegating memory is neither a virtue nor a vice in itself; its value depends on what we choose to do with the attention it frees.

Shoppers have long been trained to compare advertised prices, but a subtler practice has drawn growing scrutiny: drip pricing, in which a seller advertises a low headline price and reveals additional fees only as the buyer moves through checkout. A concert ticket acquires a service charge and a processing fee; a hotel room picks up a nightly resort fee; a budget airfare swells once a seat and a bag are added. Because each charge appears separately and late, the total is easy to underestimate, and the real price climbs <u>surreptitiously</u>.
Sellers defend the tactic as an honest way of itemizing genuine costs, arguing that customers can still inspect every fee before they pay. Consumer advocates are less forgiving. They contend that the practice takes advantage of the limits of human attention, relying on buyers who, having invested time in a purchase, are reluctant to abandon it at the final screen.
Regulators have begun to respond. A rule adopted by the US Federal Trade Commission in late 2024 requires sellers of live-event tickets and short-term lodging to display the total price, including mandatory fees, from the start, and legislators elsewhere have debated comparable measures. Economists, for their part, point out that the fees are seldom hidden outright, since they are usually listed before the buyer confirms the purchase. The difficulty, then, is less one of ____ than of timing: the information arrives, but only after the decision has largely been made.

Long before public museums opened their doors, wealthy collectors across Renaissance Europe assembled what German speakers called the Wunderkammer, or cabinet of curiosities.
(A) Yet the clutter was not without logic. Collectors sought to assemble a small model of the world within a single space, placing the products of nature side by side with the products of human ingenuity in order to reveal hidden correspondences between them. Marvels that did not fit any single category were especially prized, precisely because they blurred the lines between categories.
(B) That very ambition, however, became a weakness once natural philosophers began to favor systematic classification over wonder. Collections were gradually broken up and redistributed by discipline, and some formed the core of the first public museums, such as the Ashmolean in Oxford, which opened in 1683. The modern museum, with its orderly departments, is in this sense both the descendant and the rejection of the cabinet.
(C) These rooms, and sometimes merely cabinets, packed together objects that would later be divided among separate institutions: narwhal tusks passed off as unicorn horns, branches of coral, Roman coins, mechanical toys, and portraits of distant monarchs. To a modern visitor the effect might seem chaotic, even random.

The placebo effect is familiar to most readers: it is the phenomenon whereby a chemically inactive tablet produces real relief simply because the patient anticipates it. Far less familiar is its darker twin, the nocebo effect: negative expectations that produce real symptoms. In clinical trials, participants who receive sugar pills frequently report the very side effects listed on the consent form, such as headaches, nausea, and fatigue. (A) ____, people warned that a procedure will hurt tend to rate it as more painful than those given neutral information.
This creates an uncomfortable problem for doctors. Ethical guidelines oblige them to disclose possible adverse effects, yet the act of disclosure may itself trigger some of those effects. A striking illustration came from research on statins, drugs that lower cholesterol. In a 2020 British study, patients who had abandoned these drugs because of muscle aches were given a rotation of the real drug, identical-looking dummy pills, and months with no tablets at all. They reported nearly as much discomfort in the dummy-pill months as in the months on the real drug.
None of this means that such symptoms are imaginary or that patients should be kept in the dark. (B) ____, researchers are exploring ways of framing information that are both truthful and less alarming, for instance by stressing that the great majority of patients experience no trouble with a medication instead of focusing on the few who do.

With twelve distinct classes of color receptor, compared with the mere three that underpin human color vision, the mantis shrimp was long assumed to perceive a rainbow of colors beyond human imagining. The assumption seemed natural: more receptors ought to mean finer discrimination. When researchers in Australia put the idea to a rigorous test in 2014, however, the results were humbling for the crustacean. Trained to choose between pairs of colors, the shrimp struggled to distinguish wavelengths that differed by less than roughly twelve to twenty-five nanometers, whereas humans can often tell apart colors separated by just a few.
The researchers proposed an interesting explanation. Rather than comparing signals from different receptors, as human brains slowly do, the shrimp may simply register which receptor is most strongly stimulated, recognizing colors almost instantly instead of analyzing them. Such a system would sacrifice subtlety for speed, a sensible ____ for a predator that strikes with one of the fastest punches in the animal kingdom and has little time to deliberate.

Boredom has a poor reputation. Parents rush to rescue children from it, and adults reach for their phones at the first hint of an idle moment. The dislike runs deep. In a much-discussed 2014 study led by the psychologist Timothy Wilson, participants were asked to sit alone in a bare room with nothing to do but think for up to fifteen minutes. Many found the experience so <u>irksome</u> that they chose to give themselves a mild electric shock, a shock that many of them had earlier said they would pay to avoid. Overall, roughly two-thirds of the men and a quarter of the women pressed the button at least once.
Yet some researchers contend that boredom serves a purpose. Like hunger or pain, it may function as a signal, alerting us that our current activity has ceased to be rewarding and prompting us to seek something more meaningful. There is also tentative evidence that it can nourish creativity. In one British experiment, participants who first spent a quarter of an hour copying numbers from a telephone directory later thought of more inventive uses for a pair of plastic cups than those who had been spared the tedious task, perhaps because a restless mind begins to wander.
The implication is not that boredom should be cultivated for its own sake, but that constantly ending it with digital distraction may deprive us of the very discomfort that pushes us toward new pursuits.

For decades, discussions of climate-driven migration were framed in distant terms, with forecasts of millions displaced by rising seas at some uncertain point in the future. For the inhabitants of Tuvalu, a Pacific nation of roughly eleven thousand people scattered across low-lying atolls, the issue has never felt abstract. Most of its land lies only a few meters above sea level, and seawater already contaminates the groundwater on which crops depend.
In 2023 Tuvalu and Australia signed the Falepili Union, a treaty that, among other provisions, created a special visa pathway allowing up to 280 Tuvaluan citizens a year to settle in Australia with the right to live, work, and study there. When the first ballot for places opened in 2025, registrations vastly exceeded the number of available spots.
The agreement has been hailed as a pioneering model for nations confronting deadly environmental threats, yet it has also provoked unease. Some Tuvaluans worry that a steady departure of young people could hollow out their communities and erode a culture rooted in particular islands. The government, for its part, insists that migration is meant to be a choice rather than a mass departure, and it continues to pursue land reclamation while campaigning for its statehood and maritime boundaries to remain recognized even if its territory is eventually submerged.

Aristotle's ethics is often summarized by the phrase golden mean, but the slogan invites misunderstanding. It suggests a dull counsel of moderation, as though the virtuous person were someone who never feels anything too intensely. Aristotle meant something considerably more demanding. Each virtue, in his account, lies between two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency. Courage, for example, sits between rashness, which rushes carelessly into danger, and cowardice, which flees from it at the first sign of threat. Generosity lies between prodigality and stinginess.
Crucially, the mean is not an arithmetical midpoint fixed in advance. It is relative to us, shaped by circumstances, roles, and the particular situation. Fury may be precisely the right response to a grave injustice, whereas mild irritation would be a failure of feeling. ____, a soldier defending a city and a traveler stopped by a stranger on a dark road may experience similar fear yet be called upon to act very differently.
How, then, is anyone to identify the mean? Aristotle offers no formula. Instead, he points to practical wisdom, or phronesis, a capacity cultivated through experience and habit rather than learned from rules. We become just by performing just acts, he argues, much as we become builders by building. Virtue, on this view, is less a matter of knowing what is right in the abstract than of having trained one's perceptions and desires so that the right action comes to seem natural.

Few items of health advice are repeated as confidently as the injunction to drink eight glasses of water a day. Yet the rule's pedigree is surprisingly murky. It is often traced to a 1945 recommendation from the Food and Nutrition Board in the United States, which suggested that adults needed roughly 2.5 liters of water daily. The very next sentence, frequently omitted in later retellings, noted that most of this quantity is contained in prepared foods. Somewhere along the way, a sensible estimate of total intake hardened into a prescription for glasses of plain water.
In fact, the body obtains fluid from a wide range of sources. Fruit and vegetables are largely water, and soups, milk, and even coffee and tea contribute substantially; for habitual drinkers, the mild diuretic effect of caffeine does not cancel out the fluid these beverages supply. For most healthy adults in temperate climates, thirst is a reasonably reliable ____, prompting them to drink well before dehydration becomes hazardous.
None of this implies that hydration is trivial. Athletes exercising in the heat, outdoor laborers, and elderly people, whose sense of thirst tends to diminish with age, may need to drink deliberately rather than waiting for the urge. The point is that a single universal number obscures how much requirements vary with body size, exertion, climate, and diet. Drinking water is rarely harmful, but the eight-glass rule owes its longevity more to its memorable simplicity than to evidence.

Vertical farming once seemed poised to transform agriculture. By growing leafy greens in stacked trays under LED lights inside warehouses, start-ups promised crops free of pesticides, immune to drought, and harvested a few kilometers from the supermarkets that sold them. Venture capitalists invested billions in the industry during the late 2010s and early 2020s.
The reckoning arrived swiftly. Between 2023 and 2024, several prominent vertical-farming companies in the United States and Europe filed for bankruptcy or shut down entirely. The central difficulty was energy. A conventional farm receives its sunlight free of charge, whereas an indoor farm must pay to replace it, and when electricity prices surged after 2021, many operators found their costs (A) ____. Moreover, the crops that thrive indoors, such as lettuce and herbs, are low in calories and fetch modest prices, which limits the revenue each square meter can generate.
Advocates insist the idea is far from dead. They argue that cheaper renewable power and more efficient lighting could restore its economics, and that indoor farms make sense where arable land is scarce or the climate is extreme, as in Singapore or the Persian Gulf. Skeptics reply that the technology is likely to remain a (B) ____ rather than a substitute for fields, valuable in particular niches but incapable of feeding cities on its own.

In the late 1990s, a series of experiments seemed to reveal something fundamental about self-control: that it behaves like a muscle, growing fatigued with use.
(A) The controversy has not settled whether willpower can ever be depleted; some researchers maintain that the effect exists but is smaller and more fragile than once believed. What it has done is change how psychologists conduct research. Registering hypotheses in advance and sharing raw data, once rare practices, have become increasingly common, precisely so that a seductive idea cannot again outrun its evidence.
(B) In the best-known study, hungry participants who had been made to resist a plate of freshly baked cookies and eat radishes instead gave up sooner on an unsolvable puzzle than those who had been allowed to indulge. The researchers called the phenomenon ego depletion, and over the following decade hundreds of studies appeared to corroborate it, extending the idea to dieting, shopping, and even moral conduct.
(C) Doubts gradually accumulated, however. Many of the original studies relied on small samples, and journals were far more inclined to publish striking positive results than null findings. In 2016 a coordinated replication involving more than twenty laboratories and over two thousand participants found an effect so slight that it was statistically indistinguishable from zero.

In the second book of Plato's Republic, Glaucon recounts the legend of Gyges, a shepherd who discovers a golden ring that renders its wearer invisible whenever its setting is turned toward the palm. Armed with this power, Gyges seduces the queen, murders the king, and seizes the throne. Glaucon's purpose in telling the story is deliberately provocative. He contends that anyone who possessed such a ring, the just and the unjust alike, would eventually behave in the same way, because people refrain from wrongdoing only out of fear of being caught. Justice, on this view, is a reluctant compromise struck by <u>the weak</u>: since most of us cannot commit injustice with impunity, we agree not to commit it so that we need not suffer it.
Socrates devotes much of the remaining dialogue to a rebuttal. He argues that injustice corrupts the soul of the person who commits it, disordering its parts much as disease disorders the body, so that the unjust person is wretched whether or not anyone ever discovers the crime. Whether his answer succeeds has been debated for more than two millennia, but the question Glaucon posed retains its sting: would we remain honest if we knew that no one would ever find out?

At a growing number of airports, the boarding pass is giving way to the face. Travelers approach a camera at the gate, the system compares their image with a photograph on file, and the barrier opens within seconds. Proponents tout the technology as both faster and more secure than inspecting documents by eye, since a machine does not grow weary at the end of a long shift.
Governments have embraced it with particular enthusiasm at borders. In October 2025 the European Union began phasing in its Entry/Exit System, ____ records the fingerprints and facial images of most non-EU travelers on short stays and replaces the manual stamping of passports. In the United States, the Transportation Security Administration has expanded facial comparison at airport checkpoints, though passengers there may still decline and request a manual identity check.
Privacy advocates remain <u>wary</u>. A stolen password can be changed; a face cannot. They worry that databases assembled for convenience could be repurposed for surveillance, and that error rates, which some studies have found to differ across demographic groups, could subject certain travelers to repeated and humiliating scrutiny. Supporters reply that images are often deleted shortly after verification and that the alternative, a human officer glancing at a photograph, is hardly infallible. The debate is therefore less about whether the technology works than about who controls the data it generates, and for how long.

When people imagine how a major life event will affect them, they tend to picture the change itself and overlook what comes after it. A promotion, a new house, or a move to a sunnier city is expected to deliver lasting contentment. Psychologists who track well-being over many years, however, have documented a humbling regularity known as hedonic adaptation: after an initial surge, happiness usually drifts back toward its previous level as the novelty fades and the improvement becomes the new baseline.
The same process cushions people against misfortune. Many who suffer serious setbacks report, months later, levels of satisfaction far closer to their former state than they had predicted, although adaptation to some events, such as prolonged unemployment, appears to be slower and less complete. ____, our forecasts err in both directions, exaggerating the joy that good fortune will bring and the misery that adversity will inflict.
Researchers have proposed ways to slow the fading of pleasure. Experiences that keep changing, such as travel or the mastery of a skill, tend to resist adaptation better than possessions, which remain static. Deliberately savoring small pleasures, or pausing to imagine one's life without a cherished advantage, can also restore a measure of the delight that familiarity erodes.

The word quarantine carries the memory of a number. When the Black Death swept through Europe in the mid-fourteenth century, physicians had no conception of bacteria, yet many authorities sensed that the disease traveled with people and goods. In 1377 Ragusa, the Adriatic port now called Dubrovnik, ordered that ships arriving from infected areas must wait thirty days before their passengers and cargo could enter the city. Other harbors, Venice among them, later introduced similar rules, and the waiting time was ultimately lengthened to forty days; the Venetian phrase quaranta giorni gave English its word.
Why forty? The figure had no basis in what we would now call epidemiology. ____, it may have owed something to its resonance in Christian tradition, which associated forty days with purification, from the flood of Noah to the fast of Lent. Whatever its origin, the practice proved <u>prescient</u>: separating the possibly infected from the healthy curbed contagion even though no one could explain why.
Ports built lazarettos, isolated compounds where travelers and merchandise were detained, and where goods were aired or fumigated. Confinement was often grim and occasionally deadly, and merchants resented delays that strangled commerce. Yet the underlying principle has endured for more than six centuries, reappearing in virtually every subsequent epidemic, including the global outbreak of 2020.

Much of what we do each day is not, strictly speaking, decided. In diary studies conducted by the psychologist Wendy Wood and her colleagues, participants recorded what they were doing and thinking at regular intervals; roughly 43 percent of their actions were performed almost daily in the same context, usually while their minds were occupied with something else. Such behaviors are habits: responses triggered by cues in the environment rather than by deliberate intention.
This insight has practical implications for anyone hoping to change their conduct. Because habits are bound to context, willpower is a feeble instrument for dismantling them; a resolution made in a tranquil moment is easily overridden when the familiar cue reappears. More effective strategies tend to alter the environment itself. People who move house, for instance, often find it easier to abandon old routines, since the cues that sustained them have vanished. Adding friction to undesirable behaviors, such as keeping snacks out of sight, and removing friction from desirable ones, such as laying out running shoes the night before, can accomplish more than repeated exhortations to try harder.
New habits, meanwhile, take time to form. One frequently cited study found that the period required for a behavior to become automatic varied enormously, from a few weeks to the better part of a year.

Asked how they feel, many people reach for a handful of blunt words: good, bad, stressed, fine. The psychologist Lisa Feldman Barrett has argued that the care with which we label our emotions, a capacity she calls emotional granularity, matters more than we might suppose. A person with high granularity does not merely feel bad; she tells apart being disappointed, resentful, anxious, or homesick, much as a trained wine taster detects flavors that a casual drinker groups together as simply red wine.
This is not a mere matter of taste. Studies in this line of research have reported that people who draw finer distinctions among their negative feelings tend to cope with distress more flexibly; they are, for example, less likely to drink heavily or lash out aggressively when upset. ____, people with low granularity may treat every unpleasant state as the same general distress, leaving them with a single, often blunt, remedy. Why should naming help? One possibility is that a precise label suggests a fitting response: someone who recognizes that she is lonely rather than merely miserable knows to call a friend.
Granularity, moreover, appears to be learnable. Because emotion words are acquired through culture and conversation, enlarging one's vocabulary of feeling, whether by reading fiction, borrowing terms from other languages, or simply pausing to ask what exactly one is experiencing, may sharpen the distinctions themselves.

Some seven thousand languages are in use around the world, and linguists estimate that around forty percent of them are endangered, many with only a few elderly speakers. Because of the crisis, the United Nations declared 2022 to 2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages. Increasingly, the response is digital. Communities are recording elders' stories, building online dictionaries, and adapting smartphone keyboards to unfamiliar alphabets, so that young people can send messages in their grandparents' tongue.
Artificial intelligence has added both promise and new problems. Speech-recognition and translation tools could make <u>dwindling</u> languages usable in everyday technology, but such systems require huge amounts of recorded speech, which technology companies have sometimes sought to gather on their own terms. In New Zealand, the Māori broadcaster Te Hiku Media built its own speech-recognition tools for te reo Māori and has insisted that the recordings its community contributed remain under Māori control rather than being absorbed into commercial datasets.
Linguists caution that technology cannot replace speakers. An archive can preserve the sound of a language, but only families and schools that use it daily can keep it alive. Digital tools are best understood as aids to passing a language on between generations, not as a museum in which a language is stored after its last speaker has gone.

For decades, the standard advice about stress was simple: reduce it. Stress hormones were cast as enemies, and a pounding heart before an examination was treated as a symptom to be calmed.
(A) None of this means that chronic stress is harmless. Prolonged pressure, such as caring for a sick relative for years or enduring persistent poverty, is linked to genuine harm to health, and no change of mindset can eliminate the conditions that produce it. Reappraisal is a tool for acute challenges, not a substitute for addressing their causes.
(B) In a series of experiments, the psychologist Jeremy Jamieson and his colleagues told some participants, before a stressful task such as a mock job interview or a standardized test, that a racing pulse is a sign of the body getting ready to meet a challenge. Compared with those who received no such message, these participants often showed healthier patterns of heart activity and, in some studies, performed better.
(C) Researchers have since begun to question whether the bodily response itself is the problem. The rush of adrenaline that comes with a challenge sharpens attention and delivers oxygen-rich blood to muscles and brain, preparing the body to perform. What seems to matter is how that arousal is interpreted.

Go down a few hundred meters into the ocean and sunlight fades to nothing, yet the darkness is far from absolute. A large share of the creatures that live in the deep produce their own light. In one survey of animals filmed by remotely operated vehicles off the coast of California, roughly three-quarters of those observed in the water column were capable of bioluminescence. The glow usually arises from a chemical reaction in which a compound called luciferin is oxidized with the help of an enzyme, releasing energy as light rather than heat.
Light serves very different purposes in this dark world. The anglerfish hangs a glowing lure in front of its head to draw prey toward its jaws. Hatchetfish and some squid emit a faint glow from their bellies that matches the dim light coming from above, hiding the outline a predator below would otherwise see, a tactic known as counter-illumination. Certain tiny plankton flash when disturbed, which may act as a burglar alarm, calling in larger predators that prey on whatever is attacking them.
Because most of this light is blue or green, the colors that travel farthest through seawater, many deep-sea animals have eyes tuned to those wavelengths. A few predators, however, produce red light that most of their prey cannot ____, allowing them to illuminate a target without giving away their own position.

The promise of the smart city is attractive: sensors that time traffic lights to actual traffic, bins that report when they are full, streetlights that dim when no one is near. Each of these conveniences, however, depends on collecting data about how residents move and behave, and the question of who owns that data has proved far more contentious than the technology itself.
Toronto learned this lesson early. In 2017 the city's waterfront agency selected Sidewalk Labs, a sister company of Google, to develop a high-tech neighborhood on its eastern shoreline. The project soon became caught up in a dispute over surveillance and data governance, and in 2020 the company withdrew, citing economic uncertainty during the pandemic. (A) ____, the episode became a warning for planners elsewhere.
Regulators have since moved to draw firmer lines. The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act, adopted in 2024, largely bans police from using real-time facial recognition in publicly accessible spaces, allowing it only in a few clearly defined cases, such as searching for kidnapping victims. Some cities now publish registers of the algorithms they use and require that data be stripped of names before it is shared with private companies.
Supporters of smart technology warn that too much caution could deprive cities of genuine benefits, such as fewer traffic jams and lower energy use. (B) ____, they argue, the goal should be to govern data wisely rather than to avoid collecting it altogether.

When Emily Dickinson died in 1886, she left behind nearly 1,800 poems, fewer than a dozen of which had been published in her lifetime, and those largely without her consent. Her sister discovered the manuscripts in a locked box, many of them sewn into small hand-bound booklets. The first editions, which appeared in the 1890s, were a considerable success, but they presented a curiously <u>domesticated</u> Dickinson. Her editors regularized her punctuation, replaced her abundant dashes with commas and periods, smoothed some of her slant rhymes into conventional ones, and added titles for poems she had left untitled.
They meant no harm. They believed that readers would reject verse so unconventional and that minor corrections were the price of recognition. Yet the alterations hid exactly what made the poems distinctive. Dickinson's dashes create pauses and ambiguities that commas cannot reproduce; a line interrupted by a dash may be read in two directions at once.
Only in 1955, with an edition by the scholar Thomas H. Johnson that followed the manuscripts closely, did most readers encounter the poems in something approaching their original form. Even now, editors disagree about how to print marks that look sometimes like dashes and sometimes like slanted lines. The case illustrates a larger truth: an editor's choices, however well intentioned, shape the text we believe we are reading.

Every sports fan has witnessed it: an experienced professional, perfect in practice, misses an easy putt or a routine free throw when the championship is on the line. Psychologists call this choking under pressure, and research by Sian Beilock and others suggests that it often stems not from too little concentration but from too much of the wrong kind.
Highly practiced skills are largely automatic; an expert golfer does not consciously watch over each movement of the wrists. Under pressure, however, performers may begin monitoring and controlling actions that ordinarily run on their own, and this conscious meddling breaks up the smooth movement that skill depends on. ____, novices, whose skills are not yet automatic, are less vulnerable to this particular disruption, since they must attend to each step anyway.
Pressure can also hurt performance in a different way, by crowding working memory with worries, which is especially damaging on tasks such as mental arithmetic that require holding information in mind. Several fixes have been suggested. Some studies suggest that writing about one's anxieties shortly before an examination can free up mental resources, while athletes are sometimes taught to fix their attention on a single external target, or to occupy the mind with counting or humming, so that they do not overthink movements best left alone.

Myopia, or nearsightedness, has become very common. In parts of East Asia, surveys have found that a large majority of young adults are nearsighted, a proportion far higher than a few generations ago. Because the change has been too rapid to be explained by genetics alone, researchers have looked to the environment, and the habit that first attracted suspicion was close work such as reading and, more recently, staring at screens.
The evidence, however, increasingly points to a different cause: too little time outdoors. Children who spend more hours outside tend to be less likely to develop myopia, apparently regardless of how much they read. One leading explanation is that bright daylight, often far more intense than the illumination inside buildings, prompts the retina to release dopamine, a chemical messenger that appears to slow the lengthening of the eyeball that makes distant objects appear blurred.
Such findings have prompted policy experiments. In Taiwan, schools were encouraged to send children outdoors for two hours a day, and the share of schoolchildren with myopia, which had been climbing for decades, then began to fall. Researchers caution, however, that outdoor time chiefly helps prevent the onset of myopia rather than reversing it once established, which is why attention has turned to treatments that might slow its progression in children who are already nearsighted.
